  accept

Then provide a 2–3 sentence rationale explaining your prediction.

## Paper

## Abstract

An early event after lung injury is extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling and the formation of a provisional
matrix. While megakaryocytes and platelets (Mgk/plt) play important roles in hemostasis, their impact on
the matrix in lung injury is not fully understood. Using lung intravital microscopy, 3D large area scanning
with multiphoton confocal hybrid imaging, and label-free quantitative proteomics, the matricellular protein
thrombospondin-1 (TSP1) arising from Mgk/plt protects the lung from alveolar injury. Mgk/plt cell-specific
Thbs1 knockout (cKO) mice show increased alveolar barrier disruption with exaggerated neutrophil-
mediated injury. The cKO mice exhibit striking extracellular matrix re-organization with reduction in
basement membrane protein COL6A1 after injury. Moreover, cKEO mice increase Mgk numbers to regions
of fibrillar collagen deposition and alveolar leak. Our findings indicate Mgk/plt-derived TSP1 represents
a key mechanism of matrix stabilization by protectinNg the basement membrane from neutrophil-mediated
proteolytic damage, regulating injury severity and Mgk numbers at the alveolar interface.

---

## Introduction

Acute lung injury, clinically known as the acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), is a syndrome of
acute hypoxemic respiratory failure caused by alveolar epithelial-capillary membrane barrier disruption1,2.
A prominent feature of ARDS is an exaggerated inflammatory response often dominated by a neutrophil-
rich exudate in the airspaces3. Infection-related insults such as severe pneumonia cause direct lung
injury whereas sepsis causes an indirect form of lung injury. These two risk factors collectively account
for the majority of ARDS worldwide4, although non-infectious injury from aspiration, trauma, and
inhalational toxins also results in ARDS5. An intense inflammatory response in the airspaces of ARDS
patients occurs during the early exudative phase and is characEterized by proinflammatory cytokines and
chemokines, release of neutrophil proteases such as neutrophil elastase (NE) and metalloproteinase-9
(MMP-9), as well as their inhibitors. In addition, thNe early phase of injury is characterized by elevated
procollagen peptide III levels, a marker of collagen synthesis and dysregulated repair6,78.

Original reports in ARDS demonstrated that ECM remodeling is an early event that shifts the balance
towards fibrillar collagen I synthesis and deposition9. This early ECM remodeling event leads to altered
lung tissue mechanics after injury in an experimental rat model10. Persistent elevation in markers of
collagen synthesis in the airspace compartment is associated with ineffective lung repair and increased
risk of death in ARDS11,12. While inflammatory injury is a hallmark of clinical ARDS and thought to
contribute to matrix remodeling, whether components of the early ECM regulate the inflammatory
response and shape the outcome of alveolar injury and repair are less known.

Thrombospondin-1 (TSP1) is a matricellular protein involved in cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions and
a component of the lung ECM13. Multiple cell types produce TSP1 including Mgks and platelets,
endothelial cells13, fibroblasts14, smooth muscle cells15, type II pneumocytes16, macrophages17, and
dendritic cells18. However, platelets19 are the major source of TSP1 in circulation and store large
quantities of TSP1 in α-granules20,21. Upon platelet activation, TSP1 is liberated onto the platelet
membrane and the extracellular space22,24,25. Although direct evidence for TSP1 involvement in the
stabilization of the lung ECM is lacking, TSP1 binds collagen I23, fibrinogen/fibrin, fibronectin24, heparan
sulfate proteoglycans25, laminin26, as well as integrins such as α \beta 24 which is highly expressed by
3 1
alveolar epithelial cells27. In acute lung injury, alveolar barrier disruption leads to exposure of the
subendothelial matrix to the vascular compartment and extravasation of serum proteins, platelet proteins,
and clotting factors. Platelets and their cellular constituents are critical for the formation of the initial
provisional matrix during wound healing comprised of a loose ECM network that permits cell movement,
migration, and dynamic remodeling28,29, although platelet constituentSs that are involved in lung injury are
poorly understood. Given that Mgks and platelets are a major source of TSP1, and that TSP1 is
incorporated into the provisional matrix30,31, we sought to determine whether Mgk/plt TSP1 represents a
key mechanism of matrix stabilization, regulating neut rophil response and Mgk numbers at the alveolar
interface.

---

## Results

Intravital microscopy reveal increased alveolar barrier disruption in global Thbs1-/- reporter mice
following alveolar injury.

Our previous work demonstrated that TSP1 deletion in mice increases lung microvascular permeability
after acute pulmonary infection with Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA)19,32. Here, we used live intravital
imaging to precisely localize and quantify airspace leakage following alveolar injury.

For this purpose, reporter ROSAmT/mG mice that constitutively express cell membrane-localized td-
Tomato in cells and tissues were crossed to Thbs1-/- global KO mice. To induce experimental lung injury,
mice underwent i.t. instillation of Pseudomonas aeruginosa cell-free supernatant (PA SN). At day 1 post-
injury and just prior to imaging, mice were i.v. injected with FITC-Dextran (70 kDa) to visualize dextran
extravasation into the airspaces by live intravital microscopy (Fig. 1A). Image processing and analysis
were conducted according to the schematic pipeline illustrated in Figure 1B-F, utilizing a custom-
developed NIS-Elements General Analysis (GA3) recipe to ensure precise and reproducible
quantification. Representative raw images of lungs from vehicle treated and PA SN injured mice are
shown with alveolar parenchymal structure outlined in red and intravenously injected FITC-dextran
visualized in green (Fig. 1B), where the injured lung shows greater dispersal of FITC-dextran beyond the
alveolar boundaries. For quantification of alveolar leak, lung structure was segmented and overlaid with
a corresponding binary mask defined by the presence or absence of Td-tomato expressing cell
membrane (Fig. 1C). The resulting binary mask was inverted to identify the airspaces (Fig. 1D). The
emissions from the FITC-dextran were segmented based on the emiSssion intensity of the FITC channel
(Fig. 1E). We quantified airspace leak using area overlap analysis with a Boolean “And” statement where
the area of airspace leak (µm2) was defined as the pixels within the defined airspace mask that were also
positive (“And”) for dextran (Fig. 1F). Quantitative a nalysis confirmed that ROSAmT/mGThbs1-/- mice
exhibited significantly greater leakage of dextranI into the airspaces following alveolar injury compared to
wild-type controls (Fig. 1G).

Megakaryocyte/platelet-specifTic Thbs1 KO mice show normal platelet function

To address the cell-intrinsic role of TSP1, we generated a Thbs1 floxed allele mouse (Thbs1flox) using
CRISPR/Cas9 technology. Targeted insertion of LoxP sites in intron 3 and intron 7 led to the generation
of the floxed allele (Fig. S1A). As platelets and their precursors Mgks are a major source of TSP1,
Thbs1flox mice were subsequently bred with Cre-expressing mice under the control of the platelet factor
4 gene (PF4Cre) to obtain Mgk/platelet-specific Thbs1 knock-out (PF4CreThbs1flox KO) mice. Thrombin-
stimulated platelet releasates from the PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice showed loss of TSP1, while WT littermate
controls (PF4WTThbs1flox) displayed levels comparable to those of C57BL/6 wild-type mice (Fig. 2A).
Moreover, cell-specific deletion of TSP1 from Mgk/platelets (Mgk/plt) did not alter circulating platelet
counts (Fig. 2B) nor did it affect the surface levels of activated αIIbβ3 integrin (Fig. 2C) or P-selectin (Fig.
2D) following stimulation with various concentrations of thrombin or collagen-related peptides (CRP) (Fig.
S1B-C). Platelet aggregation responses to thrombin (Fig. S1D) and CRP (Fig. S1E) were similar between
WT and PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice. Platelet activation and aggregation were also similar between WT
littermates and PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice in response to increasing concentrations of U46619 (a
thromboxane TXA2 analog) or ADP (Fig. 2E-H). These results suggest that Mgk/plt TSP1 does not
regulate platelet activation and adhesive function.

MgK/plt TSP1 regulates neutrophil activity and matrix remodeling-related proteins to limit
alveolar barrier disruption during live bacterial infection.

In a live lower respiratory tract infection model with Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Fig. 3A), PF4CreThbs1flox
KO mice exhibited higher lung bacterial burden at day 1 post-infectionS compared to WT littermate controls
(Fig. 3B). Although global Thbs1 KO mice show significant defects in host defense during acute PA
pneumonia when compared to WT mice19,32, a more modest phenotype was observed in PF4CreThbs1flox
KO mice, suggesting that additional cellular sources o f TSP1 contribute to pulmonary host defense. To
assess the role of MgK/plt-derived TSP-1 in alvIeolar barrier integrity, we measured total BALF protein
levels. Following PA instillation, PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice exhibited significantly elevated BALF protein
levels compared to WT littermates (Fig. 3C). Notably, airspace neutrophil recruitment (Fig. 3D) were
comparable between WT and PTF4CreThbs1flox KO mice. Despite similar numbers of neutrophils in the
airspaces, PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice showed significantly higher BALF neutrophil elastase (NE) activity
(Fig. 3E) and MMP-9 levels (Fig. 3G). Moreover, airspace neutrophils from PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice
demonstrated higher levels of CD63 surface expression, a marker of degranulation (Fig. 3G-H). In the
live infection model, a gating strategy to delineate immune cell subsets in the BALF and lung showed no
differences in other cell types besides neutrophils including alveolar macrophages, eosinophils, and
monocytes between WT and PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice (Fig. S2A-D). Despite similar immune cell
numbers, PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice showed elevated levels of myeloperoxidase (MPO) and NE-DNA
complexes in the BALF, indicative of enhanced neutrophil granule release and neutrophil extracellular
trap (NET) formation (Fig. S2E-F). Levels of cytokines and chemokines involved in neutrophil responses
were similar between WT and PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice (Fig. S2G–K). Moreover, neutrophils obtained
from PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice were not developmentally altered and showed no differences in CD62L
and, \alphaM\beta2 surface levels ex vivo either at baseline or with TNF\alpha, fMLP, or A23187 stimulation (Fig. S2L-
M). The ability to form platelet-neutrophil aggregates was similar between the two groups (Fig. S2N).
Other cell types produce TSP1, in particular myeloid-derived cells, that could influence the course of
inflammation and injury in the live infection model. However, myeloid cell-specific Thbs1 KO mice
(LysMCreThbs1flox) showed no differences in lung CFU following live PA infection, BALF total protein,
BALF NE activity or composition of immune cells in BALF and lung tissue homogenates (Fig. S2O-T).
Collectively, these data strongly suggest that Mgk/plt TSP1 limits neutrophil activation within the lung
tissue microenvironment.

Given the essential role of Mgk/plts in forming the provisional matrix29,30, we explored matrix-related
proteins within the airspace compartment. We utilized mass spectrometry label-free quantitative
proteomics to compare the proteomic profile of BALF in WT and PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice. Neutrophil
degranulation was identified as the top enriched pIathway in BALF following PA infection when comparing
the differential proteomic signatures of WT and PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice (Fig. 3I). To assess the alveolar
matrix niche, we performed laser-capture microdissection (LCM) of injured alveolar tissue from WT and
PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice after live PA infection and coupled with label-free quantitative mass
spectrometry. Strikingly, differential analysis of the alveolar tissue proteomics between WT and
PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice revealed shared pathway enrichment signatures including neutrophil
degranulation, platelet activation, and ECM organization also identified in BALF (Fig. 3J). Differentially
up and down regulated proteins comparing WT and PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice in BALF and alveolar tissue
within these shared pathways feature key proteins involved in early lung injury (Fig. S3A and S3B). Within
alveolar tissue, we identify increases in neutrophil proteases ELANE (or, NE), MMP9, CTSG (or,
Cathepsin G) and markers of the provisional matrix29,33,34 fibronectin (FN1), fibrin or fibrinogen proteins
(FGA, FGB, FGG), F13A1 (which catalyze the conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin), and integrins in
PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice when compared to WT after injury (Fig. S3B). The increase in provisional matrix
proteins observed in PF4CreThbs1flox KO alveolar tissue is likely a consequence of the increased injury
and leak observed in these mice.

Loss of MgK/plt TSP1 but not endothelial TSP1 leads to increased alveolar leak with impaired
lung function following injury.

To exclude the possibility that the injury is from uncontrolled bacterial replication, we induced sterile lung
injury in WT and cKO mice using cell-free PA supernatant (PA SN)35 and evaluated microvascular
permeability by intravital imaging to visually confirm and quantify the degree of airspace leak following
injury. For this purpose, we generated PF4CreROSAmT/mG (WT) and PF4CreROSAmT/mG Thbs1flox (TSP1PF4
KO) reporter mice that constitutively express tdTomato in all cell membranes except in Mgks and
platelets which express green fluorescence protein (GFP) undeSr the control of PF4-driven Cre
recombinase. We utilized segmentation and overlay analysis of WT and TSP1PF4 KO reporter mice lungs
to quantify alveolar leak (Fig. S4A-F). At day 1 post PA SN instillation, mice were i.v. injected with CF680-
Dextran (70 kDa, cyan) and dextran extravasation into the airspaces was visualized by intravital
microscopy (Fig. 4A-B). When WT and TSP1PFI4 KO reporter mice were i.t. instilled with sterile PBS
(vehicle), dextran was visualized within the vessels and, to a limited extent, within the interstitium (Fig.
4B, left upper and lower panels). How C ever, when mice were instilled with PA SN, both WT and TSP1PF4
KO reporter mice showed wideniTng of the interstitial space and dextran extravasation into the airspaces,
whereas TSP1PF4 KO reporter mice showed significantly elevated levels of CF680-Dextran leak into the
alveolar space as measured by airspace leak area (Fig. 4C) and airspace leak intensity (Fig. 4D).
Intravital microscopy details a limited window to the lung, therefore we confirmed these findings by
quantifying the lung injury score in H&E sections (Fig. 4E-L), Evans blue (EB) dye assay to assess lung
permeability (Fig. 4M), and lung mechanics (Fig. 4N-R). PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice showed increase in
hemorrhagic injury, as evidenced by higher lung injury score after PA SN instillation when compared to
WT littermates (Fig. 4H). We did not observe differences between WT and PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice in
the ratio of neutrophils localized to either the alveolar spaces or interstitium (Fig. 4I-J). This finding is
consistent with similar neutrophil numbers found in WT and PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice after live PA
infection (Fig. 3D). The increase in lung injury score observed in the PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice after sterile
injury is driven by the alveolar edema tissue score and the alveolar septal thickness score rather than
the ratio of alveolar or interstitial PMN scores (Fig. 4K-L). This finding is consistent with the airspace
barrier leak observed by lung intravital microscopy (Fig. 4B-D). Moreover, PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice
exhibited increased lung EB extravasation following PA SN challenge when compared with WT
littermates (Fig. 4M). We next tested lung function at baseline (without vehicle) in WT and PF4CreThbs1flox
KO mice. As expected, injury reduced static compliance in both groups of mice (Fig. 4N). Forced
oscillation tests further reduced the dynamic compliance observed in PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice but not in
WT mice group, underscoring the altered lung function in the PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice after injury (Fig.
4O). At day 1 post-injury, PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice had significaSntly increased respiratory system
resistance (Fig. 4P), Newtonian resistance (Fig. 4Q), and tissue elastance (Fig. 4R). These
biomechanical changes are features of lung injury and underscore the importance of MgK/platelet-
derived TSP1 in maintaining lung function and integrity .

Previous studies identified a protective role for endothelial-derived TSP1 in limiting alveolar epithelial
injury13. To determine whether endo C thelial TSP1 contributes to maintaining alveolar barrier integrity
following PA SN challenge, we gTenerated endothelial-specific Thbs1 cKO (Cdh5CreThbs1flox) mice. Loss
of endothelial TSP1 did not significantly alter lung EB accumulation following PA SN challenge (Fig. S5A-
B) compared to WT littermates (Cdh5WTThbs1flox). Unlike MgK/platelet-derived TSP1, these findings
suggest that endothelial TSP1 does not play a major role in limiting alveolar leak or injury-associated
barrier dysfunction.

Mice deficient in MgK/platelet TSP1 show increased MgK recruitment to sites of collagen
exposure and alveolar barrier disruption.

Prior reports indicate that Mgks are localized to the lungs of human and mice36,37. Utilizing publicly
available gene expression data38, we show that the relative Thbs1 gene expression in adult lung MgK is
higher than in adult bone marrow MgK (Fig. S6A). In addition, fetal lung MgKs demonstrate higher Thbs1
gene expression than fetal liver MgKs (Fig. S6A). By lung intravital imaging, we noted striking
appearance of lung MgKs that were > 30 microns in diameter (Fig. 5A, Supplementary Movie 1). To
distinguish MgKs from platelets or platelet aggregates, we confirmed MgK by nuclear staining with DAPI
and high resolution (60X, 1.4NA) large scanning of static lung tissue by confocal microscopy (Nikon A1R)
(Fig. S6B). Advanced 3D image analysis using surface rendering tools in Imaris (Bitplane) confirmed
MgKs with nuclei (Fig. S6C). Quantitative analysis using the NIS-Elements software revealed that, under
vehicle instillation conditions, MgK events were similar in WT and TSP1PF4 KO reporter mice (Fig. 5B).
However, after PA SN-induced lung injury, TSP1PF4 KO reporter mice exhibited a significant increase in
MgK events (defined as > 30 \mu m in size) compared to WT reporter controls (Fig. 5B). The dynamic MgK
accumulation in TSP1PF4 KO reporter mice suggests dysregulated mSobilization or retention in the lung
microenvironment following injury. Lung platelet events were not different between the groups by imaging
analysis or flow cytometric analysis (Fig. S6D-I), while peripheral platelet counts dropped with injury
(Fig. S6J).

Collagen levels play a critical role in Mgk function, mediated by interactions with collagen fibers via
receptors such as GPVI and \alpha2\beta1 integrin39,40. Our BALF proteomic analysis demonstrated enrichment
of key proteins involved in both ECM degradation and collagen formation (Fig. 3I, 5C), suggesting altered
collagen or ECM componeAnt levels. Consistent with these findings, Second Harmonic Generation (SHG)
microscopy of collagen in our lung injury model revealed that fibrillar collagen was markedly increased
in TSP1PF4 KO reporter mice (Fig. 5D-F). Both the total collagen area and collagen deposition near
regions of airspace leak were higher in TSP1PF4 KO reporter mice compared to WT mice (Fig. 5G-H).
Moreover, collagen accumulation in proximity to Mgks and where Mgks localized to regions of airspace
leak were significantly elevated in TSP1PF4 KO reporter mice (Fig. 5I-J). Interestingly, Mgks were
identified in both the extravascular (Fig. 5A, and Supplementary Movie 1) and intravascular spaces (Fig.
5D), and were prominently located at the junctions of alveolar structures marked by Td-Tomato
expression (Fig. 5D). These observations were further validated by 3D large-area multiphoton/confocal
hybrid imaging (Nikon AXR MP/Confocal), which confirmed increased collagen deposition within
adventitial interstitium where Mgks accumulate in TSP1PF4 KO reporter mice lungs (Fig. 5K-L).
Collectively, these results indicate that loss of Mgk/platelet-derived TSP1 leads to increased collagen
deposition and Mgk accumulation, likely reflecting greater degree of injury and leak.

Neutrophil depletion ameliorates lung injury and increases basement membrane protein levels in
mice deficient in Mgk/platelet TSP1.

We next evaluated whether the exaggerated neutrophilic response observed in the lungs of Mgk/plt-
deficient TSP1 mice is a main driver of increased alveolar permeability following lung injury. Pre-
treatment with anti-Ly6G antibody to deplete neutrophils resulted inS a robust decrease in BALF PMN
counts and MPO release (Fig. 6A-C) and reduction of alveolar permeability similar to levels observed in
WT controls (Fig. 6D). These data demonstrate neutrophils as a major contributor to the intense barrier
disruption observed in PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice and su ggest that MgK/platelet TSP1 dampens excessive
neutrophil activation encountered at the barrier inIterface.

In parallel experiments, flow cytometric analysis was performed following anti-Ly6G antibody treatment
(Fig. 6E). While the lung neuTtrophil counts were comparable between isotype-treated WT and
PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice after PA SN injury (Fig. 6F), NE release in BALF were significantly higher in
PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice (Fig. 6G). Depleting neutrophils with anti-Ly6G antibody treatment reduced lung
neutrophil counts and BALF NE levels in PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice (Fig. 6F-G). BALF IgM levels, a
surrogate marker of lung permeability, were increased in PF4CreThbs1flox KO compared to WT mice after
injury (Fig. 6H). Analysis of live CD45+CD41+ Mgk revealed that isotype control antibody-treated
PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice exhibited higher Mgk accumulation than WT littermate controls (Fig. 6I-J),
consistent with lung intravital imaging results (Fig. 5B). Mgks were identified as large cells (FSChigh) that
were CD45+CD41+ and distinct from neutrophils (Fig. S7 and S7A2, respectively). Utilizing the same
gating strategy (Fig. S8A1) or adding lineage markers B220, GR1, and F4/80 in the “dump channel” to
separate lineage committed cells from Mgks (Fig. S8A2), both approaches revealed that the relative
numbers of CD45+CD41+ Mgk numbers increase in cKO lungs and distinct from neutrophils (Fig. S8A3)
when compared to WT after injury (Fig. S8B, S8C).

Importantly, neutrophil depletion diminished Mgk counts and BALF TSP1 levels in PF4CreThbs1flox KO
mice after injury (Fig. 6J-K). These findings suggest that Mgk counts and soluble TSP1 levels are markers
of injury severity. As Mgk can synthesize collagen that contributes to matrix regeneration in the
marrow39,40, we measured pro-COL1A1 and found that levels were increased in PF4CreThbs1flox KO after
injury but were not significantly different between PF4CreThbs1flox KO and WT mice after neutrophil
depletion (Fig. 6L). Neither depleting neutrophils nor reducing MgK numbers in PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice
limits COL1A1 synthesis and point to other cell types (i.e., fibroblastS) as major producers of collagen in
the lung. We also measured components of BALF COL4 and COL6 as these matrix proteins comprise
the alveolar basement membrane41,42 and were significantly reduced in PF4CreThbs1flox KO by BALF
proteomics (Figure S3A, ECM organization heatmap) . While PF4CreThbs1flox KO and WT mice showed
similar levels of BALF COL4A1 with injury, COL6A1 levels were significantly reduced in the
PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice (Fig. 6M-N). Moreover, neutrophil depletion increased COL4A1 and COL6A1
levels in lung injury (Fig. 6M-N). These findings strongly support the concept that Mgk/plt TSP1 prevents
degradation of the alveolar baTsement membrane, specifically COL6A1, from neutrophil-mediated
proteolytic injury (Fig. 6O).

## Methods

Sex as a biological variable

Both male and female mice aged-matched (7–22 week olds) were Sused for studies involving experimental
lung injury. We did not observe sex differences in the outcomes measured. Additional information is
provided in the Supplementary Source Data file.

Mice

C57BL/6J (WT, stock #000664), CC57BL/6-Tg(Pf4-icre)Q3Rsko/J (PF4Cre, stock #008535), and
B6.129P2-Lyz2tm1(cre)Ifo/J (LyTsMCre, stock #004781) mice were originally obtained from the Jackson
Laboratories (Bar Harbor, ME) and maintained in the animal facility of University of Pittsburgh and
Washington University in St. Louis. TSP-1 floxed (Thbs1flox) and full body TSP-1 deficient mice (Thbs1-/-)
were generated at the University of Pittsburgh Transgenic and Gene Targeting and Innovative
Technologies Development Cores using CRISPR/Cas9 technology. Briefly, single stranded
oligodeoxynucleotide (ssODN) templates were used to introduce LoxP and BamHI restriction enzyme
sites between exons 3 and 4, and exons 7 and 8 of the Thbs1 gene by homologous directed repair at
the position of the double strand break (DSB) induced by Cas9 nuclease. Genotyping using PCR flanking
the LoxP sites and BamHI restriction digest identified founder mice carrying the Thbs1 floxed allele that
was confirmed by genomic sequencing. The founder mice were backcrossed to the C57Bl/6J mice for 6
generations and homozygous founder colonies of Thbs1fl/fl mice were subsequently established. Thbs1fl/fl
mice were bred with PF4Cre mice to obtain a megakaryocyte and platelet specific TSP-1 knockout mouse
line (PF4CreThbs1flox) and their WT littermate controls (PF4WTThbs1flox).

For intravital imaging, PF4CreThbs1flox were bred with the ROSAmT/mG mice to obtain
PF4CreROSAmT/mGThbs1flox (TSP1PF4 reporter) and PF4CreROSAmT/mGThbs1flox (WT reporter) reporter
mouse line. Additionally, ROSAmT/mG mice were bred with Thbs1-/- mice to obtain a full body reporter
mouse line deficient for TSP-1 (Thbs1-/-ROSAmT/mG). ROSAmT/mG mice were used as reporter WT controls.
To evaluate the role of endothelial TSP-1 in tissue resiliency, Thbs1fl/fl mice were bred with constitutive
Cdh5Cre mice (B6.FVB-Tg(Cdh5-cre)7Mlia/J, JAX stock #006137), kindly provided by Dr. Kyunghee Choi
(Washington University) to obtain endothelial specific TSP-1 knockouSt mouse line (Cdh5CreThbs1flox) and
their WT littermate controls (Cdh5WTThbs1flox). Each mouse line used in this study was co-housed in the
same vivarium and fed the same chow for at least 4 weeks prior to in vivo experiments. All experimental
protocols were reviewed and approved by the IACUC at the University of Pittsburgh and Washington
University in St. Louis.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa live bacterial lung infection and sterile injury models.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa PA14 strain was grown overnight at 37ºC, 2,500 x g in 3 mL of Luria-Bertani
(LB) broth (Sigma-Aldrich L3522) to reach an optical density (OD) = 0.5-0.6 which yielded ~1 x 109 – 5 x
109 CFU/mL. Next, 100 µL of the preparation was resuspended in 10 mL of sterile PBS to reach a stock
inoculum concentration of 1 x 107 – 5 x 107 CFU/mL. Mice were anesthetized with isoflurane in an
anesthesia chamber and intratracheal (i.t.) inoculation with 100 µL of the stock for a final inoculum of ~1-
5 x 106 CFU of PA1419,32,35. In indicated experiments, PA14 strain was grown overnight (16-18 hours) at
37ºC, 2,500 x g in 3 mL of LB broth. The overnight culture was then filtered through a 0.22 \mu m sterile
filter to obtain PA14 cell free SN that was delivered i.t. to induce sterile lung injury35. Mice were i.t.
inoculated with 30% cell free PA SN at 100 \mu l volume. Depending upon the experiment, sex- and age-
matched mice were delivered either live bacteria or PA SN by i.t. delivery. Mice were euthanized after 1
day for tissue processing.

Lung tissue and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) collection.

The trachea was cannulated using an 18 G catheter, and the left lung was ligated at the hilum with 2-0
silk suture. BALF from the right lung was subsequently obtained from mice by instilling a first lavage of
600 µL of sterile cold 1x PBS/EDTA (0.6 mM), followed by 3 more lavages of 500 µL each (final volume
of 2.1 mL). BALF cells were pelleted by centrifugation at 300 x g for 15 min for flow cytometry and the
cell-free supernatant was collected and stored in -80oC until further use19,32. BALF measurements
included total BALF protein content (Pierce™ BCA Protein Assay Kit, Thermofisher), free NE activity,
myeloperoxidase (MPO) levels, free DNA NE-DNA complex and untargeted proteomics (LC/MS).

Peripheral platelet counts.

Circulating platelets of mice were counted using the Hemavet 950 (Drew Scientific). 100 µL of blood from

Platelet aggregation assay.

Platelets from PF4CreThbs1flox mice and WT littermates were washed in HEPES-Tyrode buffer and

For assessment of platelet activation, mouse platelets were washed in HEPES-Tyrode buffer and treated

Quantitative proteomics.

BALF from PA infected WT, Thbs1-/-, PF4CreThbs1flox and PF4WTThbs1flox mice were collected at day 1
post-infection and centrifuged at 300 x g for 15 min to separate the pellet from the supernatant. BALF
supernatants were processed by the mass spectrometry and proteomics facility at the Ohio State
University for liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) analysis.

Protein Digestion via Strap. S-trap was used for the digestion. Briefly, 20% SDS in 200 mM TEAB
(Triethylamonium bicarbonate) was spiked into the sample to make the final concentration of 5% SDS in
50mM TEAB. 5 µL of 50 mM ABC containing 5 µg/µL DTT was added, and the sample was incubated at
65 ºC for 15 min followed by addition of 5 µL of 50 mM ABC containing 15 µg/µL iodoacetamide
(incubated at RT for 15 min in the dark). Samples were then acidified by adding 12% phosphoric acid
(1:10 v/v acid to sample). For every 25 µL of samples, 165 µL of TEAB (Triethylammonium bicarbonate,
1M)/MeOH (10:90 v/v) was added and then loaded to S-trap for further washes. Samples was centrifuged
at 4000 x g for 3 min (4C) to remove supernatant. 150 µL of TEAB (Triethylamonium bicarbonate,
1M)/MeOH (10:90 v/v) was added to the trap as wash solution and the trap was washed 3 times. After
the final wash, sequencing grade trypsin dissolved in 50 mM TEAB was added and digested O/N at 37
ºC. The following day, peptides were eluted from the trap by adding 40 µL of 50mM TEAB, 0.1% FA and
0.1% FA in Acetonitrile (50:50), sequentially. The sample was pooled together and dried in a vacufuge
and resuspended in 20 µL of 50 mM acetic acid. Peptide concentrSation was determined by nanodrop
(A280 nm).

Orbitrap Fusion. Nano-liquid chromatography-nanospr ay tandem mass spectrometry (Nano-LC/MS/MS)
of protein identification was performed on a TIhermo Scientific orbitrap Fusion mass spectrometer
equipped with an nanospray FAIMS Pro™ Sources operated in positive ion mode. Samples (2 µg) were
separated on an easy spray nano column (EASY-Spray™ HPLC Columns, C18 3 µ 100A, 75 µm X 250
mm Thermo Scientific) using a 2D RSLC HPLC system from Thermo Scientific. Each sample was
injected into the trap coluAmn (Acclaim™ PepMap™ C18, 3µ 100A, 75 µm X 20 mm Thermo Scientific)
and desalted with 0.1% Formic Acid in water for 5 minutes. The injector port was then switched to “inject”
and the peptides were eluted off of the trap onto the column. Mobile phase A was 0.1% Formic Acid in
water and acetonitrile (with 0.1% formic acid) was used as mobile phase B. Flow rate was set at 300
nL/min. Mobile phase B was increased from 2% to 16% in 105 min and then increased from 16-25% in
10 min and again from 25-85% in 1 min and then kept at 95% for another 4 min before being brought
back quickly to 2% in 1 min. The column was equilibrated at 2% of mobile phase B (or 98% A) for 15 min
before the next sample injection.

MS/MS data was acquired with a spray voltage of 1.95 KV and a capillary temperature of 305 °C was
used. The scan sequence of the mass spectrometer was based on the preview mode data dependent
TopSpeed™ method: the analysis was programmed for a full scan recorded between m/z 375-1500 and
a MS/MS scan to generate product ion spectra to determine amino acid sequence in consecutive scans
starting from the most abundant peaks in the spectrum in the next 3 seconds. To achieve high mass
accuracy MS determination, the full scan was performed at FT mode and the resolution was set at
120,000 with internal mass calibration. Three compensation voltage (cv=-50, -65 and -80v) were used
for samples acquisition. The AGC Target ion number for FT full scan was set at 4 x 105 ions, maximum
ion injection time was set at 50 ms and micro scan number was set at 1. MSn was performed using HCD
in ion trap mode to ensure the highest signal intensity of MSn spectraS. The HCD collision energy was set
at 32%. The AGC Target ion number for ion trap MSn scan was set at 3.0E4 ions, maximum ion injection
time was set at 35 ms and micro scan number was set at 1. Dynamic exclusion was enabled with a
repeat count of 1 within 60s and a low mass width and high mass width of 10 ppm.

Database searching. All MS/MS samples were analyzed using Mascot (Matrix Science, London, UK;
version 2.7.0). Mascot was set up to search the Common_Contamination_Proteins-
cRAP_LZ_20190813.fasta; UnTiprot_Mouse_Reviewed_08272021_20210827 database (unknown
version, 17195 entries) assuming the digestion enzyme strict trypsin. Mascot was searched with a
fragment ion mass tolerance of 0.50 Da and a parent ion tolerance of 10.0 PPM. Carbamidomethyl of
cysteine was specified in Mascot as a fixed modification. Deamidated of asparagine and glutamine and
oxidation of methionine were specified in Mascot as variable modifications.

Criteria for protein identification. Scaffold (version Scaffold_5.0.1, Proteome Software Inc., Portland, OR)
was used to validate MS/MS based peptide and protein identifications. Peptide identifications were
accepted if they could be established at greater than 95.0% probability to achieve an FDR less than 1.0%
by the Scaffold Local FDR algorithm. Protein identifications were accepted if they could be established
at greater than 98.0% probability to achieve an FDR less than 1.0% and contained at least 2 identified
peptides. Protein probabilities were assigned by the Protein Prophet algorithm. Proteins that contained
similar peptides and could not be differentiated based on MS/MS analysis alone were grouped to satisfy
the principles of parsimony.

Relative quantitation using label free spectral counting. Protein abundance was quantified using protein
spectral counts in the BALF of C57Bl/6J WT (n=2), Thbs1-/- (n=2), PF4CreThbs1flox (n=4)
and PF4WTThbs1flox (n=4) mice one day 1 post-infection with Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Fold change
abundance and statistical testing were performed using a two sample Welch t-test after log2 plus one
transformation of the protein spectral counts to compare expressioSn between PF4CreThbs1flox and WT
mice. Protein accessions were mapped to gene identifiers using STRING52. Reactome pathway
enrichment was performed using over-representation analysis with hypergeometric testing of statistically
significant proteins (p < 0.05) between WT and PF4Cre Thbs1flox mice.

For alveolar tissue proteomics, experiments were conducted at the WashU Mass Spec Core, Mass
Spectrometry Technology Access Center at the McDonnell Genome Institute, Washington University in
St. Louis. Briefly, laser capture Tmicrodissection was performed on histopathological sections targeting
regions of alveolar injury within the lung day 1 post i.t. inoculation of PA in PF4creThbs1flox and WT mice.
After laser capture, regions of injury were digested and processed for LC-MS/MS. Mass spectrometry
samples were quantified using label free quantification (LFQ) via data-independent acquisition (DIA) and
mapped against the mouse database in Spectronaut for DIA-LFQ analysis. The precursor filter algorithm
in Spectronaut was utilized to retain proteins with valid label free quantification values and the t-test was
performed for comparisons between WT and PF4creThbs1flox mice. Multiple test correction was performed
using the Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Protein accessions were mapped to gene identifiers using
STRING. Reactome pathway enrichment was performed using over-representation analysis with
hypergeometric testing of statistically significant proteins between WT and PF4creThbs1flox mice.

Intravital lung imaging and quantitative image analysis.

ROSAmT/mG and ROSAmT/mG Thbs1-/- mice were intratracheally (i.t.) instilled with vehicle (PBS) or 30%
Pseudomonas aeruginosa supernatant (PA SN). At 24 h, mice were intraperitoneally (i.p.) anesthetized
using a cocktail of Ketamine (100 mg/kg body weight) and Xylazine (10 mg/kg body weight), and the left
lung was exposed and immobilized. In initial experiments utilizing RosamT/mG and RosamT/mGThbs1-/- mice
to confirm alveolar barrier permeability and quantify dextran extravasation from the circulation to the
airspaces, 70 kDa FITC-dextran (5 mg/ml, ThermoFisher, D1822) was administrated intravenously just
prior to visualization of the lung by multiphoton excitation (MPE) microscopy (Nikon A1R MP). FITC and
TdTomato were excited with the two-photon excitation wavelength 8S90 nm and emissions collected at
480 nm and 560 nm, respectively. Images were analyzed using NIS Elements (Nikon Inc.). The airspace
was identified by segmenting the cell membranes (TdTomato+) and inverting the binary mask to demark
the alveoli. FITC extravasation into the airspace was e stimated based on FITC+ area and the intensity of
the FITC emissions within the alveoli. Septal thicKness was estimated by overlaying a regular series of
horizontal and vertical test lines across each image and measuring the median distance between alveoli.

We determined the impact oTf platelet/megakaryocyte (Mgk)-specific TSP-1 on alveolar barrier
permeability as well as platelet events, Mgks, and collagen fibers surrounding areas of airspace leak by
multi-photon imaging. To evaluate the contribution of platelet/MgK TSP-1 on alveolar barrier integrity,
PF4CreROSAmT/mGThbs1flox and PF4CreROSAmT/mG mice were challenged with vehicle (PBS) or 30% PA
SN by i.t. administration. At 24 h post-injury, mice were anesthetized i.p. with a cocktail of Ketamine (100
mg/kg body weight) and Xylazine (10 mg/kg body weight), intubated, ventilated, and the left lung was
exposed and immobilized. To visualize the pulmonary vasculature and spatially localize airspace leak,
mice were intravenously injected with 70 kDa cyanine-based dye CF680-Dextran (5mg/mL; biotium) just
prior to imaging by Nikon A1R multi-photon microscope equipped with a 20X (1.0NA) water immersion
optic. GFP+ platelets and Mgks were visualized on the background of tdTomato+ alveolar membrane.
Fibrillar collagen was imaged using second harmonic generation (SHG) microscopy. All analysis was
performed using NIS Elements (Nikon Inc.). The airspace was identified by segmenting the cell
membranes based on emission intensity (TdTomato+) and inverting the binary mask to demark the
alveoli. Segmentation of platelet and MgK events was based on the intensity of the GFP emissions and
filtering of discrete objects based on size. Platelet events were defined as GFP+ structures < 4-6 microns
in size. MgKs were defined as GFP+ structures > 30 microns in size with visible nucleus. For each
parameter, 4-5 images from each mouse were analyzed and averaged to obtain a composite value for
each individual mice.

Lung Tissue processing and injury score

For left lung inflation, the right lung hilum was identified and secured with silk suture. Mouse trachea was
cannulated by gently passing a 20 G needle into the trachea Eand secured with 2-0 silk suture. The left
lung was inflated using 1% low melting agar at 20 cm H O pressure with a 10 mL syringe attached to a
2
digital manometer. The inflated lung was carefully Nremoved from the thorax and placed in ice cold PBS
to solidify the agar and then immersed in 4% paraformaldehyde overnight for fixation. Samples were
processed, embedded in paraffin, and secLtioned at 4 μm. Slides were stained by a standard H&E staining
protocol (Histowiz, Long Island City, NY). Whole-slide scanning (40×) was performed on an Aperio AT2
(Leica Biosystems). Lung section images were used to score the degree of lung injury using a
modification of a histological grading scheme53. Briefly, whole lung sections were scored randomly in 10
magnified fields (40 X) to count neutrophils in both the alveolar and interstitial compartments to yield the
alveolar neutrophil: total neutrophil ratio and the interstitial neutrophil: total neutrophil ratio. Alveolar
neutrophil and interstitial neutrophil score per field were graded as none = 0, 1-5 =1, >5 =2. Further,
alveolar protein debris and septal thickness were graded as component C (none = 0, 1 = 1, >1 = 2) and
component D (<2x = 0, 2-4x = 1, >4x = 2), respectively. The composite lung inury score was calculated
for each mouse lung section: [(20 x A) + (14 x B) + (7 x C) + (2 x D) /10], where A = airspace neutrophils,
B = interstitial neutrophils, C = proteinaceous debris filling airspaces, D = alveolar septal thickness.

Neutrophil depletion studies.

PF4CreThbs1flox and PF4WTThbs1flox mice were i.p. injected with 200 µg anti-Ly6G (clone 1A8 rat IgG2a,
k, BioLegend) or isotype control (RTK2758, Rat IgG2a, κ, BioLegend) at -24 h and at 0 h when mice
were i.t. inoculated with PA SN (30%). At 24 h post-instillation with PA SN, BALF was collected and
neutrophil depletion was assessed by cell differential counting and MPO production by ELISA (R&D
DY3667). Lung permeability was assessed by quantifying the content of total protein in the BALF
(Pierce™ BCA Protein Assay Kit, Thermofisher).

Respiratory mechanics studies.

Mice were anesthetized with a ketamine/xylazine/acepromazine cocktail (ketamine 90 mg/kg, xylazine
10 mg/kg, acepromazine 2 mg/kg, IP). Mice was trachePotomized with an 18-gauge blunt metal cannula
(typical resistance of 0.18 cmH2O s ml−1) which was secured with a nylon suture. The mouse was then
connected to the flexiVent computer-controlled piston ventilator (SCIREQ) via the cannula, which was
attached to the FX adaptor Y-tubing. Mechanical ventilation was initiated, and a dose of paralytic
vecuronium bromide (2 mg/kg) wIas administered to mice to prevent breathing efforts against the
ventilator and during measuRrements. Mice were ventilated using default settings, and respiratory
mechanics were assessed using the forced oscillation technique using the flexiVent operating software
(flexiWare version 8.2). In brief, the Static compliance (Cst), dynamic compliance (Crs) respiratory
system resistance (Rrs), Newtonian resistance (Rn), and tissue elastance (H) were measured using
forced oscillation maneuvers, at baseline and with increasing concentrations of methacholine (Mch; 0 =
PBS; 2, 4, 8, 16, 25, and 50 mg/ml) aerosol generated with an in-line nebulizer. Data was exported from
the flexiVent operating software (flexiWare version 8.2)54,55. The results were presented at baseline and
with increasing concentration of methacholine.

Megakaryocyte Thbs1 tissue specific expression analysis.

For Megakaryocyte single cell and tissue specific gene expression, tissue specific differentially
expressed gene lists in adult and fetal megakaryocytes were downloaded from the supplemental data of
Yeung, et. al. under the Gene Expression Omnibus accession number GSE15257438. Thbs1 expression
was assessed for differential expression between adult megakaryocyte populations residing in the lung
in comparison to those residing in the bone marrow as well as in fetal megakaryocyte populations
residing in the lung in comparison to those residing in the liver.

Statistics

Parametric t tests or one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed for data that were normally
distributed. For data that were not normally distributed, a non-parametric analysis using a two-tailed
Mann-Whitney U test for single comparisons and KruskaEll-Wallis for multiple comparisons was
performed. For cytokine production, the data was log transformed and a two tailed t test analysis was
used. A two-way ANOVA test with multiple compaNrison was performed to evaluate platelet aggregation
across time. Repeated measures (RM) one-way or two-way ANOVA was applied for paired samples
under different conditions. Statistical sLignificance was assigned for P <0.05. Comparisons were
performed using the GraphPad Prism software, version 10.6.1.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

Summary
This is an exciting paper from an excellent group. The primary novel finding is that platelet and megakaryocyte TSP1 plays a
major role in lung injury. They show data on barrier function, structural changes, and inflammation. The paper is clearly
written and the figures are nice. The biggest issue with the manuscript is that the main message does not really follow the
data. What I mean is, the authors focus here on permeability and barrier dysfunction but the data supporting this are not very
convincing. They also have some very cool data on neutrophil function in cKO mice and these findings are underdeveloped.
I have a high level of enthusiasm for the main message but the details of the story don’t entirely hold together. I have some
specific suggestions to improve the manuscript below.
Comments
1. With the focus on lung barrier function, it would be helpful to include more traditional measures of lung edema such as
BAL IgM and/or lung wet to dry weight ratio. In a prior JCI Insight publications, the authors do show BAL protein in these
transgenic mice which does help. This is important because there are dramatic structural abnormalities in the alveolar wall
that make assessment of edema formation challenging.
2. Along these same lines, the intravital microscopy images are beautiful but it’s not clear that they provide additional
information beyond more standard measures of barrier dysfunction and edema formation. In other words, the authors don’t
really explore the spatial aspect of edema formation that is provided by intravital microscopy.
3. The term “conditional knockout” is usually used for constructs that can be turned on with exposure to doxycycline,
tamoxifen, etc. The transgenic mouse is better described as a constitutive cell specific knockout.
4. In figure 5, the cKO vehicle treated lungs look quite different from the WT lungs. This raises concern for potential
developmental or structural effects of platelet TSP1. Could the authors show flexivent data at baseline from the cKO mice?
The flexivent data shown is fold change and does not allow for assessment of baseline structural differences between WT
and cKO. The data in figure 6 showing differences in baseline collagen heighten this concern.
5. In figure 7, the only data supporting a role for plt TSP1 in lung structure/barrier function is panel D. All other panels simply
show the effects of knocking out neutrophils on the function of neutrophils. G and H actually suggest that there is no
relationship between neutrophils and structural changes in TSP1 cKO.

### Reviewer 2

Overall this is an interesting study that adds knowledge to our understanding of lung injury and the role that
Mks and platelets have in the injury pathogenesis. There is interesting and meaningful data. Most of my critique revolves around
gaining a better understanding of the Mk/platelet and PMN interface.
1. Fig 1 and 2 are basically establishing the model for the reader. This is really important to show, but could be reduced to a
single figure with the rest of the data in supplemental files.
2. The platelet activation data is not sufficient to conclude the cKO mice have no defect in response. Higher and lower doses
of the agonists chosen as well as adding thromboxane and ADP as stimuli should be included for completeness.
3. The BALF data in Figure 3 is intriguing and leads to more questions about direct effects of platelets. WT and cKO mice
have similar PMN numbers in the BALF, yet the immune/injury markers are different. Do the authors have data regarding
PMN functions? Can they rule out that developmentally or in the circulation that PMNs in the cKO mice are not altered?
There is abundant literature that platelets affect immune cell functions and differentiation so this should be ruled in or out as
a mechanism.
4. Without validation not sure what Fig 4 is adding to the manuscript. Is just a list at this point.
5. The authors in Fig 7G indicate that the lung Mks are CD45/CD41+. These could be immune cells with adherent platelets.
This should be clarified experimentally.
6. The increase in lung Mks following injury is intriguing - are these intra or extra vascular? Is there any change in post-injury
platelet counts?
7. Do lung Mks express more thrombospondin compared to bone marrow Mks?

### Reviewer 3

The authors present a very nice story describing acute alveolar injury model where by megakaryocyte and platelet
production of thrombospondin-1 appears to play a key role in limiting neutrophil activation, megakaryocyte accumulation and
lung injury. Interestingly, animals that have Tsp-1 deficient megakaryocyte/platelets have an altered ECM in the lungs. I think
this represents an exciting area of research that capitalises on a growing interest in immune-ECM cross-regulation in health
and disease and hence will be of interest to many fields. Data analysis is well described and presented in detail and I think
the authors have done a good job here.
There are a few points that I think need better clarifying or describing, in particular centred around the term provisional
matrix. Also I think it would be important to show or least mention whether the immune phenotype of these cKO mice are
normal in the lung injury model – particularly focusing on cells like macrophages which might produce Tsp1 and therefore
influence the findings especially if changed in cell number in the lungs.
Comments
• Typically, the provisional matrix is described as a matrix largely devoid of collagens, yet in this study you are using
collagen as main indicator of a provisional matrix. I just wonder whether you need to provide further background to the
provisional matrix and perhaps also talk about how other molecules (e.g. Fn1, Vtn etc) are upregulated in cKO mice versus
WT. Why was the focus on collagen and collagen-1? In line with this, whilst the data is compelling, I’m not convinced it
points specifically to Tsp-1 “stablising” the provisional matrix – I feel this needs a bit more explanation or perhaps the
authors should pair back the wording a little?
• In relation to point above, for proteomic analysis looking at ECM molecules in BAL, it was interesting to see less Col4, Col6
etc, things that are expressed in the alveoli basement membrane in cKO v WT; also correlates with higher neutrophil
elastase levels. This isn’t specifically discussed, but is Tsp1 from platelets/megakaryocytes preventing degradation of the
basement membrane and hence preventing lung injury which may explain the change in collagen 1? Maybe a discussion
and/or schematic model (graphical abstract) of mechanism would be useful?
• For the cKO mice, the authors show levels of Tsp-1 from platelets. What are total TSP1 levels in the lungs/BAL of these
mice, ie. how much of the Tsp1 is from platelets/megakaryocytes. Are other cells compensating for a loss of Tsp1, are there
defects in other immune cells (e.g macrophages/monocytes) in cKO v WT that might influence the findings?
• Just wondering whether the authors examined neutrophil localisation? Neutrophil numbers in the BAL didn’t change but
markers of activation increased in cKO vs WT mice. Are these neutrophils more concentrated around the damaged alveoli?
• Size of the alveoli in vehicle WT v cKO mice look very different in Fig 5. During the steady state, are the function/structure
of the alveoli compromised in these mice even before they are challenged? Also looks to be more collagen in the steady
state in cKO mice – which may fit with these observations?
Minor considerations
• Approach to data analysis in Figure 1 is great. It might also be worth showing a representative overlay of segmented areas
in WT v cKO mice to really highlight the changes visually
• I would consider putting colour labels on the images in the figures so people don’t have to read the figure legends
everytime to see what colour represents what cell or protein

### Reviewer 4

General Comments
In the manuscript NCOMMS-25-26357 “Megakaryocyte/platelet-derived thrombospondin-1 stabilizes the early provisional
matrix in lung injury by exercising spatioltemporal control of neutrophil function and matrix remodeling”, the authors
demonstrate protein thrombospondin-1 (TSP1) protects the lung from acute alveolar injury using MgK/plt Thbs1 conditional
knockout mice.
My comments are specific to the proteomic portion of the manuscript.
Specific Comments

2. Shotgun proteomics terminology has been updated to label-free quantitation proteomics to reflect more accurately the
