lung intravital microscopy and analysis provide. It may have not been clear from Figure 1 that we are doing
more than visualizing and quantifying airspace leak and edema. Not only does this method identify where the
leak is, this approach allowed us to identify Mgks in the lung, spatially co-localize leak with Mgks, quantify
collagen by SHG, overlaying the SHG and lung structures and cells of interest to discover that Mgks localize to
regions of collagen deposition at sites of airspace leak (old Figure 6A-J, new Figure 5A-B, 5D-J). In response
to Reviewer 3’s request, we created overlay images comparing WT and cKO to highlight the innovative
imaging analysis performed (Revised Fig. S4). In response to Reviewer 1 and 2’s queries, we now include a
short video to show the dynamic process in real time that identifies the Mgks and their localization in relation to
the vasculature (new Figure 5A, and accompanying Suppl video 1).
Results section:
“We utilized segmentation and overlay analysis of WT and TSP1PF4 KO reporter mice lungs to quantify alveolar
leak (Fig. S4A-F).”
“Interestingly, Mgks were identified in both the extravascular (Fig. 5A, and Suppl Video 1) and intravascular
spaces (Fig. 5D), and were prominently located at the junctions of alveolar structures marked by Td-Tomato
expression (Fig. 5D).”
3. The term “conditional knockout” is usually used for constructs that can be turned on with exposure to
doxycycline, tamoxifen, etc. The transgenic mouse is better described as a constitutive cell specific knockout.
Response: Thank you for the comment. We have clarified the reference of cKO from “conditional KO” to “cell-
specific KO”. We now mention Mgk/plt Thbs1 KO mice (PF4cre Thbs1flox) by name throughout the manuscript to
avoid confusion. When referring to the reporter mice (PF4CreROSAmT/mGThbs1flox), we use the nomenclature
TSP1PF4 KO reporter mice. We have also made use of experimental schematic figures to orient the reader to
which mice are being used.
4. In figure 5, the cKO vehicle treated lungs look quite different from the WT lungs. This raises concern for
potential developmental or structural effects of platelet TSP1. Could the authors show flexivent data at baseline
from the cKO mice? The flexivent data shown is fold change and does not allow for assessment of baseline
structural differences between WT and cKO. The data in figure 6 showing differences in baseline collagen
heighten this concern.
Response: Thank you for raising these concerns. In response to Reviewer 1’s query, we performed new
Flexivent experiments at baseline (without vehicle instillation) as well as with forced oscillation technique using
cKO and WT littermates (Fig. 4N-R). There are no significant differences in baseline lung mechanics between
cKO and WT mice. Given the complexity of the graphics now shown, we split out static and dynamic lung
compliance in order to address the reviewer’s concern. As expected, injury reduced static compliance in both
groups of mice (new Fig. 4N). Methacholine challenge further reduced dynamic compliance in cKO mice but
not in WT mice group, underscoring the altered lung function in cKO mice after injury (new Fig. 4O). As
requested, the Flexivent data is now shown in actual unit measurements. Old Figure 5B showed differences in
alveolar size of WT reporter versus cKO reporter mouse lungs with vehicle instillation. We now confirm that the
scalebars for all images depicted in new Figure 4B as 100 microns. For enhanced clarity, we have replaced the
figure of the WT vehicle-treated control image (left upper panel of new Figure 4B) using a different field from
the same mouse within the same experiment.
Results section: “We next tested lung function at baseline (without vehicle) in WT and PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice.
As expected, injury reduced static compliance in both groups of mice (Fig. 4N). Forced oscillation tests further
reduced the dynamic compliance observed in PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice but not in WT mice group, underscoring
the altered lung function in the PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice after injury (Fig. 4O).”
5. In figure 7, the only data supporting a role for plt TSP1 in lung structure/barrier function is panel D. All other
panels simply show the effects of knocking out neutrophils on the function of neutrophils. G and H actually
suggest that there is no relationship between neutrophils and structural changes in TSP1 cKO.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the comment. To address Reviewer 1 and 3’s comments regarding lung
structure/barrier function, we provide new data showing the levels of alveolar basement membrane proteins
COL4 and COL6 in cKO mice following neutrophil depletion or with isotype control Ab (new Fig. 6M-N). COL4
and COL6 are both structural matrix proteins that comprise the lung basement membrane that were identified
in the BALF proteomics of cKO mice compared to WT littermates after injury (Figure 5C and S3A, ECM
organization). Notably, COL6 levels are reduced in cKO mice, and neutrophil depletion restores COL6 to levels
observed in WT littermates. As COL6 has been previously reported as a substrate of NE, the findings support
the concept that Mgk/plt TSP1 shields the basement membrane matrix protein COL6A1 from neutrophil-
mediated proteolytic damage and thereby protects against barrier disruption. In the response to query 1 by
reviewer 1, BALF IgM levels were measured, and the data are now provided (new Fig. 6H).
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
Overall this is an interesting study that adds knowledge to our understanding of lung injury and the role that
Mks and platelets have in the injury pathogenesis. There is interesting and meaningful data. Most of my
critique revolves around gaining a better understanding of the Mk/platelet and PMN interface.
1. Fig 1 and 2 are basically establishing the model for the reader. This is really important to show, but could be
reduced to a single figure with the rest of the data in supplemental files.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the positive comments. Based on Reviewer 2’s suggestion, the CRISPR
strategy used to generate the floxed mice (old Figure 2A-C) are now shown as Suppl Figure 1A. Based on
Reviewer 3’s positive comments, we have retained Figure 1 to illustrate the segmentation analysis that is
critical for understanding the novelty of our methods.
2. The platelet activation data is not sufficient to conclude the cKO mice have no defect in response. Higher
and lower doses of the agonists chosen as well as adding thromboxane and ADP as stimuli should be included
for completeness.
Response: Thank you for the comment. Please note that higher and lower doses of agonists thrombin and
CRP were previously included in prior Fig. S1A-B, now presented in new Fig. S1B-C. To address Reviewer 2’s
concerns, we performed additional experiments that include cKO and WT mouse platelet responses at
baseline and with increasing concentrations of thromboxane (U46619, a TXA2 analog) or ADP. We examined
platelet aIIbb3 activation, P-selectin surface expression, and platelet aggregation as readouts (new Figure 2E-
H). Given the importance of this negative data and for completeness, we provide the data in revised Figure 2.
3. The BALF data in Figure 3 is intriguing and leads to more questions about direct effects of platelets. WT and
cKO mice have similar PMN numbers in the BALF, yet the immune/injury markers are different. Do the authors
have data regarding PMN functions? Can they rule out that developmentally or in the circulation that PMNs in
the cKO mice are not altered? There is abundant literature that platelets affect immune cell functions and
differentiation so this should be ruled in or out as a mechanism.
Response: To address Reviewer 2’s comments, we performed new experiments to show cKO and WT
neutrophil responses at baseline and with either TNFa, fMLP, or A23187 stimulation are similar, as is the ability
to form platelet-neutrophil aggregates (New Fig. S2L-M). We used CD62L shedding, aMb2 surface expression,
and platelet-neutrophil aggregate formation as readouts. We found no differences in cKO and WT neutrophil
function ex vivo, further supporting the idea the lung tissue microenvironment having a role in regulating
neutrophil function.
4. Without validation not sure what Fig 4 is adding to the manuscript. Is just a list at this point.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this comment and have removed old Fig. 4. In the revised manuscript,
we combined the relevant portions of the BALF proteomics data from old Fig. 4 into new Fig. 3I, 3K and Fig.
S3. In response to Reviewer 3 comments, we provide data from additional experiments involving label-free
quantitation proteomics of alveolar parenchymal tissue obtained by laser capture microdissection. The alveolar
tissue was obtained after live infection. Notably, there is striking similarity in the enrichment pathway analysis
of the BALF and alveolar tissue proteomics (new Fig. 3I and 3J). We also validated the increase in neutrophil
degranulation and BALF MMP-9 shown in the BALF proteomics (new Fig. 3K) by measuring BALF MMP-9
levels by ELISA (new Fig.3F). Moreover, the proteomics data showing increased BALF MMP-9 and alveolar
tissue NE levels corroborate the exaggerated neutrophil activation markers observed in cKO mice (new Fig.
3E-H).
Results section: “Moreover, neutrophils obtained from PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice were not developmentally
altered and showed no differences in CD62L and, aMb2 surface levels ex vivo either at baseline or with TNFa,
fMLP, or A23187 stimulation (Fig. S2L-M). The ability to form platelet-neutrophil aggregates was similar
between the two groups (Fig. S2N).”
5. The authors in Fig 7G indicate that the lung Mks are CD45/CD41+. These could be immune cells with
adherent platelets. This should be clarified experimentally.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the comment. Please note that old Figure 7G (now new Fig. 6I-J)
identifying lung MgKs as CD45/CD41+ utilized a gating strategy where we gated on large cells and excluded
smaller cells such as neutrophils (new Fig. S7). To clarify this approach experimentally, we performed new
experiments showing the lung MgKs identified by FSC and CD45+/CD41+ surface markers are separate from
CD45+CD11c-CD11b+Ly6G+ neutrophils (new Fig. S8(3)). In these new experiments, we used the prior gating
strategy where we gate on large cells and identify MgKs as CD45/CD41+ (new Fig. S8(1)) and compare the
same findings using a “dump channel” to exclude cells from the CD3, B220, Gr1, F4/80, or CD11b lineage from
large cells that are Lineage negative (Lin-) CD45/CD41+ identified as MgKs (new Fig. S8(2)). Regardless of
the approach taken (i.e., whether or not Lin- markers in the dump channel used), the CD45/CD41+ Mgk
numbers increase in cKO lungs when compared to WT after injury (new Fig. S8B-C).
Results section: “Mgks were identified as large cells (FSChigh) that were CD45+CD41+ and distinct from
neutrophils (Fig. S7A1 and S7A2, respectively). Utilizing the same gating strategy (Fig. S8A1) or adding
lineage markers B220, GR1, and F4/80 in the “dump channel” to separate lineage committed cells from Mgks
(Fig. S8A2), both approaches revealed CD45+CD41+ Mgk numbers increase in cKO lungs and distinct from
neutrophils (Fig. S8A3) when compared to WT after injury (Fig. S8B, S8C).”
6. The increase in lung Mks following injury is intriguing - are these intra or extra vascular? Is there any change
in post-injury platelet counts?
Response: The Mgks localize to both intravascular and extravascular compartments. We now provide a new
image and corresponding video clip to show that MgKs are extravascular (new Fig. 5A, and Suppl video 1).
The lung intravital static images (old Figure 6C-F) identify intravascular MgKs in regions of collagen deposition
and barrier leak (new Fig. 5D-F). The large tissue scanning by confocal clearly identify Mgks within the
interstitium (old Fig. 6K-N, now new Fig. 5L indicated by blue arrows). The post-injury platelet counts in the
peripheral blood are reduced after injury in both WT and cKO mice (new Fig. S6J).
Results section: “Interestingly, Mgks were identified in both the extravascular (Fig. 5A, and Suppl Video 1)
and intravascular spaces (Fig. 5D), and were prominently located at the junctions of alveolar structures
marked by Td-Tomato expression (Fig. 5D).”
“The dynamic MgK accumulation in TSP1PF4 KO mice suggests dysregulated mobilization or retention in the
lung microenvironment following injury. Lung platelet events were not different between the groups by imaging
analysis or flow cytometric analysis (Fig. S6D-G), while peripheral platelet counts (defined as Lin-CD45-CD41+
small cells) dropped with injury (Fig. S6H-J).”
7. Do lung Mks express more thrombospondin compared to bone marrow Mks?
Response: This is an interesting question. We attempted to quantify surface as well as intracellular TSP1 in
lung MgKs and compare to bone marrow MgKs by flow cytometry. We were unable to address the question on
the protein level, as we encountered technical limitations due to non-specific labeling using three different
antibody clones. However, we were able to download publicly available data from the article by Yeung, et al
comparing lung Mgks to bone marrow Mgks, as well as fetal lung Mgks to fetal liver Mgks in mice2. We show
that the relative Thbs1 gene expression in the lung is higher in both adult and at the fetal stage (new Fig. S6A).
Results section: “Utilizing publicly available gene expression data, we show that the relative Thbs1 gene
expression in adult lung MgK is higher than in adult bone marrow MgK (Fig. S6A). In addition, fetal lung MgKs
demonstrate higher Thbs1 gene expression than fetal liver MgKs (Fig. S6A).”
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors present a very nice story describing acute alveolar injury model where by megakaryocyte and
platelet production of thrombospondin-1 appears to play a key role in limiting neutrophil activation,
megakaryocyte accumulation and lung injury. Interestingly, animals that have Tsp-1 deficient
megakaryocyte/platelets have an altered ECM in the lungs. I think this represents an exciting area of research
that capitalises on a growing interest in immune-ECM cross-regulation in health and disease and hence will be
of interest to many fields. Data analysis is well described and presented in detail and I think the authors have
done a good job here.
There are a few points that I think need better clarifying or describing, in particular centred around the term
provisional matrix. Also I think it would be important to show or least mention whether the immune phenotype
of these cKO mice are normal in the lung injury model – particularly focusing on cells like macrophages which
might produce Tsp1 and therefore influence the findings especially if changed in cell number in the lungs.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer comments. The term provisional matrix was originally described from
the wound healing literature. However, the provisional matrix in the lung after injury is poorly understood.
Based on the reviewer’s comments, we present new data from laser capture microdissection of alveolar
parenchymal tissue and label-free quantitation proteomics from these regions of interest (new Fig. 3J, 3L and
S3B). We also note the striking similarity in the enrichment pathway analysis between the BALF and alveolar
tissue proteomics in the live infection model (new Fig. 3I-J). Our response is further detailed under
“Comments” section below. Regarding the reviewer’s comment about the immune phenotype of the Mgk/plt
Thbs1 cKO mice, the immune profile is not significantly different from WT littermates in the live infection model.
We now provide the immune cell subsets in the Mgk/plt Thbs1 cKO versus wildtype mice in the BALF and lung
after live PA infection (new Fig. S2C-D). To further address the reviewer’s concern, we also provide new data in
myeloid-specific Thbs1 cKO mice (LysMcreThbs1flox) (new Fig. S2O-T). These mice do not show any
differences in CFU following live PA infection, BALF total protein, BALF NE activiy or immune cell subsets in
BALF and lung tissue homogenates.
Comments
1. Typically, the provisional matrix is described as a matrix largely devoid of collagens, yet in this study you are
using collagen as main indicator of a provisional matrix. I just wonder whether you need to provide further
background to the provisional matrix and perhaps also talk about how other molecules (e.g. Fn1, Vtn etc) are
upregulated in cKO mice versus WT. Why was the focus on collagen and collagen-1? In line with this, whilst the
data is compelling, I’m not convinced it points specifically to Tsp-1 “stablising” the provisional matrix – I feel
this needs a bit more explanation or perhaps the authors should pair back the wording a little?
Response: We thank the reviewer for these insightful comments. As the reviewer points out, the provisional
matrix is largely devoid of collagens and is comprised of fibrin, fibronectin, platelets, integrins, and
inflammatory cells. To directly assess the lung matrix niche, we performed laser-capture microdissection (LCM)
of injured alveolar tissue from cKO and WT mice after live PA infection. We now provide a description of the
provisional matrix in the Results section.
Results section: “To assess the alveolar matrix niche, we performed laser-capture microdissection (LCM) of
injured alveolar tissue from WT and PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice after live PA infection and coupled with label-free
quantitative mass spectrometry. Strikingly, differential analysis of the alveolar tissue proteomics between WT
and PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice revealed shared pathway enrichment signatures including neutrophil
degranulation, platelet activation, and ECM organization also identified in BALF (Fig. 3J). Differentially up and
down regulated proteins comparing WT and PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice in BALF and alveolar tissue within these
shared pathways feature key proteins involved in early lung injury (Fig. S3A and S3B). Within alveolar tissue,
we identify increases in neutrophil proteases ELANE (or, NE), MMP9, CTSG (or, Cathepsin G) and markers of
the provisional matrix29,33,34 fibronectin (FN1), fibrin or fibrinogen proteins (FGA, FGB, FGG), F13A1 (which
catalyze the conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin), and integrins in PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice when compared to WT
after injury (Fig. S3B). The increase in provisional matrix proteins observed in PF4CreThbs1flox KO alveolar
tissue is likely a consequence of the increased injury and leak observed in these mice.”
To the reviewer’s point regarding collagen, collagen has been shown to be an early marker of matrix
remodeling in human ARDS. Increased collagen synthesis (in particular, fibrillar collagen such as COL1) in the
BALF of ARDS patients is associated with increased mortality. Collagen’s prominence in human ARDS and our
data identifying increased fibrillar collagen deposition in regions of airspace leak by lung intravital imaging (old
Fig. 6C-F, new Figure 5D-J) and by large area scanning of lung tissue using MPE/confocal hybrid imaging
prompted us to focus on collagen and COL1. Based on our new LCM proteomics data and the Reviewers’
comments, we have revised the manuscript to focus on other collagens in addition to pro-COL1A1. We now
clarify the role of TSP1 in protecting structural basement membrane protein COL6 from neutrophil-mediated
proteolytic damage (new Fig. 6N). Please see below response to query
2. In relation to point above, for proteomic analysis looking at ECM molecules in BAL, it was interesting to see
less Col4, Col6 etc, things that are expressed in the alveoli basement membrane in cKO v WT; also correlates
with higher neutrophil elastase levels. This isn’t specifically discussed, but is Tsp1 from
platelets/megakaryocytes preventing degradation of the basement membrane and hence preventing lung injury
which may explain the change in collagen 1? Maybe a discussion and/or schematic model (graphical abstract)
of mechanism would be useful?
Response: To address the reviewer’s comment, we measured BAL COL6 levels during injury as this matrix
protein is significantly reduced in cKO by BALF proteomics (new Fig. S3B, ECM organization heatmap). We
now validate that BALF COL6A1 levels are indeed reduced in the cKO mice compared to WT mice by ELISA,
and that neutrophil depletion restores COL6A1 levels in lung injury (new Fig. 6N). These findings strongly
support the concept that Mgk/plt TSP1 prevents degradation of the matrix protein COL6A1, a key constituent of
the alveolar basement membrane, from neutrophil-mediated lung injury. We pared back the wording “stabilizes
the provisional matrix” to suggest TSP1 ‘shields’ the matrix by preventing proteolytic degradation of the
basement membrane matrix protein COL6A1. As a result of this exciting finding, we have revised the title of the
manuscript as well as sections of the abstract, results, and discussion to highlight the novel finding. In addition,
we now provide a graphical abstract of the mechanism in new Figure 6O.
Results section: “We also measured components of BALF COL4 and COL6 as these matrix proteins comprise
the alveolar basement membrane41,42 and were significantly reduced in PF4CreThbs1flox KO by BALF
proteomics (Figure S3A, ECM organization heatmap). While PF4CreThbs1flox KO and WT mice showed
similar levels of BALF COL4A1 with injury, COL6A1 levels were significantly reduced in the PF4CreThbs1flox KO
mice (Fig. 6M-N). Moreover, neutrophil depletion increased COL4A1 and COL6A1 levels in lung injury (Fig.
6M-N). These findings strongly support the concept that Mgk/plt TSP1 prevents degradation of the alveolar
basement membrane, specifically COL6A1, from neutrophil-mediated proteolytic injury (Fig. 6O).”
Title: “Megakaryocyte/platelet-derived thrombospondin-1 regulates neutrophil function and matrix remodeling
by stabilizing basement membrane COL6A1 in lung injury”
Abstract: “…These cKO mice exhibit an early airspace proteomic signature featuring neutrophil degranulation,
platelet activation, and extracellular matrix organization pathways with reduction in basement membrane
protein COL6A1 after injury. In response to the increased injury, the cKO mice display increased Mgk
recruitment to areas of fibrillar collagen deposition in regions of alveolar leak and extending into the adventitial
interstitium. Depleting neutrophils restores barrier integrity in cKO mice, reduces lung Mgk numbers, and
increases COL6A1 levels. Thus, Mgk/plt-derived TSP1 represents a key mechanism of matrix stabilization by
protecting the basement membrane from neutrophil-mediated proteolytic damage, regulating injury severity
and Mgk numbers at the alveolar interface.”
Discussion section:
“Our findings show Mgk/platelet-derived TSP1 protects the alveolar basement membrane by preventing the
matrix protein COL6A1 from neutrophil-mediated proteolytic damage and limiting Mgk recruitment to regions of
alveolar leak.”
“In contrast, PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice showed significant reductions in the basement matrix protein COL6 and
neutrophil depletion increased both COL4 and COL6 levels in lung injury. The degradation of the basement
membrane COL6 may be driving new fibrillar collagen synthesis in PF4CreThbs1flox KO mice that are
susceptible to lung injury.”
3. For the cKO mice, the authors show levels of Tsp-1 from platelets. What are total TSP1 levels in the
lungs/BAL of these mice, ie. how much of the Tsp1 is from platelets/megakaryocytes. Are other cells
compensating for a loss of Tsp1, are there defects in other immune cells (e.g macrophages/monocytes) in cKO
v WT that might influence the findings?
Response: The reviewer correctly points out that cKO mice express TSP1, as other cells besides Mgks and
platelets are still able to make TSP1 following injury. To address the reviewer’s question, we measured TSP1
levels by proteomics. In the BAL fluid, uninjured cKO and WT mice show minimal TSP1 expression based on
LC-MS/MS data. Because TSP1 levels are not significantly different in BALF by proteomics, they do not show
up in the heatmap comparisons of cKO:WT. At 24 h post-injury, we also confirmed TSP1 levels in the BAL fluid
of cKO and WT mice and do not see a difference by ELISA (Fig. 6K). By alveolar parenchymal tissue
proteomics, TSP1 levels are increased in cKO compared to WT lungs (new Fig. S3B) which may reflect the
compensatory increase in TSP1 release by other cell types. Our proteomic findings show that under basal
conditions, there is minimal TSP1 release in the BALF. We did not compare TSP1 levels from different cell
sources in vivo during acute injury which is beyond the scope of this manuscript. However, global Thbs1 KO
mice have a more pronounced phenotype than Mgk/plt Thbs1 KO mice in terms of host defense, cytokine
production, and immune cell recruitment3. This implies other cellular sources of TSP1 exert a compensatory
effect in host defense but not alveolar barrier integrity which is plt/MgK TSP1 specific. Please note that neither
the LysMcreThbs1flox (Fig. S2O-T) nor the Cdh5creThbs1flox (Fig. S5) show impaired alveolar barrier integrity
during infectious or sterile lung injury, respectively. We speculate surface bound TSP1 on plts/Mgks are
involved in dampening neutrophil proteolytic activity given their spatial proximity to neutrophils at the site of
lung injury. We have added this perspective to the Discussion section.
Discussion section: “Previous data have shown that TSP1 is surface bound on activated platelets and
undergoes a conformational change that enables enhanced interactions with integrins4. In addition, activated
neutrophils have been shown to express surface bound neutrophil proteases such as NE and cathepsin G that
retain their catalytic activity, allowing for finer control of enzymatic degradation and tissue infiltration5.”
4. Just wondering whether the authors examined neutrophil localisation? Neutrophil numbers in the BAL didn’t
change but markers of activation increased in cKO vs WT mice. Are these neutrophils more concentrated
around the damaged alveoli?
Response: Please see our response to Reviewer 1, comment 1 regarding the lung histology scoring of lungs
of cKO vs WT mice in the live infection model. As part of the lung histology scoring, we evaluated neutrophils
localized to the alveolar space and interstitium in cKO and WT mice. We did not observe differences in
neutrophil localization in the alveolar spaces or interstitium in cKO when compared to WT mice (new Fig. 4H-
L). This finding implies that TSP1 regulates neutrophil activation rather than neutrophil numbers or recruitment.
6. Size of the alveoli in vehicle WT v cKO mice look very different in Fig 5. During the steady state, are the
function/structure of the alveoli compromised in these mice even before they are challenged? Also looks to be
more collagen in the steady state in cKO mice – which may fit with these observations?
Response: Please see our response to Reviewer 1, Query 4. Old Figure 5B showed differences in alveolar
size of WT reporter versus cKO reporter mouse lungs with vehicle instillation. We have replaced the figure of
the WT vehicle-treated control image (left upper panel of new Figure 4B) using a different field from the same
mouse within the same experiment. We now confirm that the scalebars for all images depicted in new Figure
4B as 100 microns. To address whether there was any baseline structural differences that could affect lung
function, we performed new Flexivent experiments at baseline (without vehicle) as well as with forced
oscillation technique using cKO and WT littermates (Fig. 4N-R). There are no significant differences in baseline
lung mechanics between cKO and WT mice. As expected, injury reduced static compliance in both groups of
mice (new Fig. 4N). Given the complexity of the graphics now shown, we split out static and dynamic lung
compliance in order to address the reviewer’s concern. Methacholine challenge further reduced dynamic
compliance in cKO mice but not in WT mice group, underscoring the altered lung function in cKO mice after
injury (new Fig. 4O). The Flexivent data is now shown in actual unit measurements. Please note that the
increase in collagen shown in new Fig. 5G are not in steady state but following vehicle instillation and PA SN.
Minor considerations
7. Approach to data analysis in Figure 1 is great. It might also be worth showing a representative overlay of
segmented areas in WT v cKO mice to really highlight the changes visually
Response: We thank the reviewer for the excellent suggestion. We now provide a segmentation analysis
showing a representative overlay of lung images in WT and cKO mice during injury. This is provided in new
Fig. S4.
8. I would consider putting colour labels on the images in the figures so people don’t have to read the figure
legends everytime to see what colour represents what cell or protein
Response: We have now added color labels on the images in the figures for added clarity.
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
General Comments
In the manuscript NCOMMS-25-26357 “Megakaryocyte/platelet-derived thrombospondin-1 stabilizes the early
provisional matrix in lung injury by exercising spatioltemporal control of neutrophil function and matrix
remodeling”, the authors demonstrate protein thrombospondin-1 (TSP1) protects the lung from acute alveolar
injury using MgK/plt Thbs1 conditional knockout mice.
My comments are specific to the proteomic portion of the manuscript.
Response: We appreciate the constructive comments of the reviewer. As requested, we have revised the
manuscript to clarify the queries related to the proteomic assays.
Specific Comments
1. Overall, I thought the method section was lacking. Speaking to the proteomic section only (including the
supplemental methods), there is inadequate information on how the proteomic samples were prepared,
analyzed by mass spec, which mass spectrometer was used, and how the data was analyzed and by what
program.
Response: We have included the full detail of the methods used in our experiments, including sample
preparation for proteomics, the mass spectrometer used, how data was analyzed and by which software. We
also include new experimental data with alveolar parenchymal tissue proteomics. Please refer to the new
supplementary methods and Fig. 3 and Fig. S3 legends.
Quantitative proteomics for BALF in Supplementary methods: “Protein Digestion via Strap. S-trap was used for
the digestion. Briefly, 20% SDS in 200mM TEAB (Triethylamonium bicarbonate) was spiked into the sample to
make the final concentration of 5% SDS in 50mM TEAB. 5 µL of 50 mM ABC containing 5 µg/µL DTT was
added and the sample was incubated at 65 °C for 15 min followed by addition of 5 µL of 50 mM ABC
containing 15 µg/µL iodoacetamide (incubated at RT for 15 min in the dark). Samples were then acidified by
adding 12% phosphoric acid (1:10 v/v acid to sample). For every 25uL of samples, 165uL of TEAB
(Triethylammonium bicarbonate, 1M)/MeOH (10:90 v/v) was added and then loaded to S-trap for further
washes. Samples was centrifuged at 4000g for 3 min (4C) to remove supernatant. 150uL of TEAB
(Triethylamonium bicarbonate, 1M)/MeOH (10:90 v/v) was added to the trap as wash solution and the trap was
washed 3 times. After the final wash, sequencing grade trypsin dissolved in 50mM TEAB was added and
digested O/N at 37 °C. The following day, peptides were eluted from the trap by adding 40uL of 50mM TEAB,
0.1% FA and 0.1% FA in Acetonitrile (50:50), sequentially. The sample was pooled together and dried in a
vacufuge and resuspended in 20 µL of 50 mM acetic acid. Peptide concentration was determined by nanodrop
(A280nm).
Orbitrap Fusion. Nano-liquid chromatography-nanospray tandem mass spectrometry (Nano-LC/MS/MS) of
protein identification was performed on a Thermo Scientific orbitrap Fusion mass spectrometer equipped with
an nanospray FAIMS Pro™ Sources operated in positive ion mode. Samples (2ug) were separated on an
easy spray nano column (EASY-Spray™ HPLC Columns, C18 3µ 100A, 75µm X250mm Thermo Scientific)
using a 2D RSLC HPLC system from Thermo Scientific. Each sample was injected into the trap column
(Acclaim™ PepMap™ C18, 3µ 100A, 75µm X20mm Thermo Scientific) and desalted with 0.1% Formic Acid in
water for 5 minutes. The injector port was then switched to “inject” and the peptides were eluted off of the trap
onto the column. Mobile phase A was 0.1% Formic Acid in water and acetonitrile (with 0.1% formic acid) was
used as mobile phase B. Flow rate was set at 300nL/min. mobile phase B was increased from 2% to 16% in
105 min and then increased from 16-25% in 10 min and again from 25-85% in 1 min and then kept at 95% for
another 4 min before being brought back quickly to 2% in 1 min. The column was equilibrated at 2% of mobile
phase B (or 98% A) for 15 min before the next sample injection.
MS/MS data was acquired with a spray voltage of 1.95 KV and a capillary temperature of 305 °C is used. The
scan sequence of the mass spectrometer was based on the preview mode data dependent TopSpeed™
method: the analysis was programmed for a full scan recorded between m/z 375-1500 and a MS/MS scan to
generate product ion spectra to determine amino acid sequence in consecutive scans starting from the most
abundant peaks in the spectrum in the next 3 seconds. To achieve high mass accuracy MS determination, the
full scan was performed at FT mode and the resolution was set at 120,000 with internal mass calibration.
Three compensation voltage (cv=-50, -65 and -80v) were used for samples acquisition. The AGC Target ion
number for FT full scan was set at 4 x 105 ions, maximum ion injection time was set at 50 ms and micro scan
number was set at 1. MSn was performed using HCD in ion trap mode to ensure the highest signal intensity of
MSn spectra. The HCD collision energy was set at 32%. The AGC Target ion number for ion trap MSn scan
was set at 3.0E4 ions, maximum ion injection time was set at 35 ms and micro scan number was set at 1.
Dynamic exclusion is enabled with a repeat count of 1 within 60s and a low mass width and high mass width of
10ppm.
Database searching. All MS/MS samples were analyzed using Mascot (Matrix Science, London, UK; version
2.7.0). Mascot was set up to search the Common_Contamination_Proteins-cRAP_LZ_20190813.fasta;
Uniprot_Mouse_Reviewed_08272021_20210827 database (unknown version, 17195 entries) assuming the
digestion enzyme stricttrypsin. Mascot was searched with a fragment ion mass tolerance of 0.50 Da and a
parent ion tolerance of 10.0 PPM. Carbamidomethyl of cysteine was specified in Mascot as a fixed
modification. Deamidated of asparagine and glutamine and oxidation of methionine were specified in Mascot
as variable modifications.
Criteria for protein identification. Scaffold (version Scaffold_5.0.1, Proteome Software Inc., Portland, OR) was
used to validate MS/MS based peptide and protein identifications. Peptide identifications were accepted if they
could be established at greater than 95.0% probability to achieve an FDR less than 1.0% by the Scaffold Local
FDR algorithm. Protein identifications were accepted if they could be established at greater than 98.0%
probability to achieve an FDR less than 1.0% and contained at least 2 identified peptides. Protein probabilities
were assigned by the Protein Prophet algorithm (Nesvizhskii, Al et al Anal. Chem. 2003;75(17):4646-58).
Proteins that contained similar peptides and could not be differentiated based on MS/MS analysis alone were
grouped to satisfy the principles of parsimony.
Relative quantitation using label free spectral counting. The spectral count of each protein identified in the
dataset were used to quantify the abundance of each protein in the BALF of WT (n=2), Thbs1-/- (n=2),
PF4CreThbs1flox (n=4) and PF4WTThbs1flox (n=4) mice at 1 day post-infection. Data was Log normalized and

Response: We thank the reviewers for their time in carefully reviewing the revision and their encouraging

REVIEWERS' COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors did a very nice job responding to my questions and suggestions and the manuscript is much
improved as a result. I do have two additional suggestions.
1. In figure 4G, The PF4.Cre/Thbs1.Flox PA SN lungs appear to have airways filled with blood, Did these mice
experience alveolar or airway hemorrhage? Can the authors explain this observation?
Response: The reviewer astutely comments on the alveolar and airway hemorrhage shown in Figure 4G. We
previously published the live PA infection model where global TSP1 KO mice show increased barrier disruption
in lung injury compared to WT1,2. In a subsequent manuscript, we show that mice with low platelets (Mpl-/-) exhibit
significant alveolar hemorrhagic injury 2, prompting us to examine the role of Mgk/plt cell specific TSP1 KO mice.
Based on the findings reported in the current manuscript, we suggest the alveolar hemorrhage [editorial note:
confidential information redacted] and airway hemorrhage observed in mice deficient in megakaryocyte and
platelet TSP1 are due to barrier disruption from matrix degradation of basement membrane protein COL6. COL6
is found not only in the alveolar basement membrane but also along perivascular and peribronchiolar regions of
the lung3,4. [editorial note: confidential information redacted]. Although beyond the scope of this manuscript,
we modified the results section to add the point about increased hemorrhage in the Mgk/plt cKO mice.
[editorial note: confidential figure redacted]

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
Overall the authors have done an excellent job addressing reviewers concerns. I just ask for some clarification
and further lung Mk quantification and characterization analysis.
The authors state -"gating strategy where we gated on large cells and excluded smaller cells such as
neutrophils". Lung megakaryocytes are not all large cells, they are largely 2N, so a size based exclusion shown
in Fig S7 there are likely a large number of Mks that are missing from the analysis. It is strongly suggested that
additionally markers such as CD42c be added to the lung flow panel, less size exclusion employed and more
negative/dump channel markers used in the analysis. This will greatly improve the overall rigor and make readers
more confident in the proper cell identities.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the comment and raising this important point. We performed both size
exclusion and negative/dump channel markers to remove the possibility of platelet-neutrophil aggregates as a
confounder in the lung Mgk quantification as this was a concern previously raised by the same reviewer. We
agree that CD42c is another specific Mgk and platelet marker. However, adding CD42c together with CD41 will
exclude non-activated Mgk which is not the goal of the current experiment. We utilized size exclusion as a second
method to minimize the counting of platelet-neutrophil aggregates in addition to the use of negative/dump
channel markers (i.e., B220, CD3, Gr1, F4/80) to exclude B cell, T cell, myeloid cell, and macrophage
populations, as shown in Figure S7. Using the two methods together to exclude platelet-neutrophil or platelet-
monocyte aggregates improved rigor, albeit at the expense of identifying higher numbers of potential lung Mgks.
Please note that our focus was relative and not absolute quantification of the lung Mgk, as indicated in
supplemental Figure S8 legend. Our main question pertains to whether lung Mgk numbers increase after injury
in the lung which we believe we have effectively addressed. To the reviewer’s point, we have emphasized in the
results section that our focus is relative quantification of lung Mgk. As suggested by the reviewer, we will add
CD42c to our panel for future studies focusing on the role of lung Mgks in injury.
Original results section: “Mgks were identified as large cells (FSChigh) that were CD45+CD41+ and distinct from
neutrophils (Fig. S7 and S7A2, respectively). Utilizing the same gating strategy (Fig. S8A1) or adding lineage
markers B220, GR1, and F4/80 in the “dump channel” to separate lineage committed cells from Mgks (Fig.
S8A2), both approaches revealed CD45+CD41+ Mgk numbers increase in cKO lungs and distinct from
neutrophils (Fig. S8A3) when compared to WT after injury (Fig. S8B, S8C).”
Revised results section: “Mgks were identified as large cells (FSChigh) that were CD45+CD41+ and distinct from
neutrophils (Fig. S7 and S7A2, respectively). Utilizing the same gating strategy (Fig. S8A1) or adding lineage
markers B220, GR1, and F4/80 in the “dump channel” to separate lineage committed cells from Mgks (Fig.
S8A2), both approaches revealed that the relative numbers of CD45+CD41+ Mgk numbers increase in cKO lungs
and distinct from neutrophils (Fig. S8A3) when compared to WT after injury (Fig. S8B, S8C).”
